entries.test: Public comparisons of competing AI developers’ technology, training data, and durable competitive advantages would test whether technical and data similarity eliminates their moats.
entries.note: “No AI company” broadens the contextual claim about competing AI developers to every AI company.

entries.test: Public market-share evidence showing a company capturing 90% of the relevant AI market while competitors lack moats would falsify the prediction.
entries.note: There is no deadline; the absence of moats is an explicit condition.

entries.test: Public pricing, margins, and competitive-position evidence would test whether the absence of clear winners produces price wars and commodity pricing rather than monopoly pricing.
entries.note: The sentence primarily asserts an economic causal relationship.

entries.test: AI developers’ disclosed investment costs and eventual profits under sustained intense competition would show whether their spending exceeded the returns it generated.
entries.note: “Everyone investing in AI” expands the referent beyond the competing developers. The outcome depends on the competitive regime established in the preceding argument.

entries.test: Public financial evidence of sustained commercial profitability in the LLM industry would falsify the claim that it will never be commercially viable.
entries.note: Marcus explicitly attributes the argument to Garran and endorses it as compelling.

entries.test: Published pricing changes and customer surveys or cancellation evidence would show whether ending unlimited plans caused widespread customer reconsideration.
entries.note: The claim combines a current pricing change with an undated prediction about its customer effects.
“The economics don’t make sense” has no shared decisive test. The normalization also strengthens “might fall apart” into “will fall apart.”

entries.test: Public index-inclusion records and subsequent investment returns would show whether Anthropic and OpenAI enter indices and impose losses on index trackers and retail investors.
entries.note: “Same will happen” adopts the preceding quoted scenario as Marcus’s own prediction.

entries.test: Public investment-flow, ownership, and loss records would show whether 2026 left retail investors and index funds bearing the losses from AI investments.
entries.note: The prediction identifies 2026, which has not ended at evaluation. It leaves the collapse and retrospective recognition dates unspecified.
